stem: You find yourself in a state of panic and your sympathetic nervous system is taking over. Which of the following actions describe the correct physiology in this state?

options.html: Your sympathetic nervous system releases norepinephrine which increases motility and secretion of the GI tract
Your sympathetic nervous system releases acetylcholine which increases motility and secretion of the GI tract
Your sympathetic nervous system releases acetylcholine which decreases motility and secretion of the GI tract
Your sympathetic nervous system releases substance P which decreases motility and secretion of the GI tract
Your sympathetic nervous system releases norepinephrine which decreases motility and secretion of the GI tract

answer:
The correct answer is E.

The sympathetic system releases norepinephrine which in turn decreases motility, secretions, blood flow, and delays gastric emptying. In a relaxed state the parasympathetic system relies on acetylcholine to increase motility and secretion to process food throughout the GI tract.

stem: Several different hormones affect secretion and motility within the gastrointestinal tract. Which statement below is true?

options.html: Cholecystokinin reduces the rate of emptying of the stomach.
Motilin reduces motility within the digestive tract.
Gastrin reduces the secretion of gastric acid in the stomach.
Secretin reduces the secretion of bicarbonate from the pancreas.

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Cholecystokinin is a hormone that induces the pancreas to secrete digestive enzymes, and the stomach to reduce the rate of emptying. Motilin increases gut motility; gastrin increases the secretion of gastric acid; and secretin increases the secretion of bicarbonate from the pancreas.

Goblet cells secrete mucus into the small intestines
Paneth cells secrete serotonin into the small intestines
Chief cells secrete trypsinogen into the stomach

The correct answer is B.

Parietal cells secrete HCl and intrinsic factors. Goblet cells secrete mucus into the small intestine. Paneth cells secrete antibacterial factors into the small intestine (enteroendocrine cells secrete serotonin into the small intestines). Chief cells secrete pepsinogen into the stomach. Note that trypsinogen is secreted by the pancreas.

stem: Which of the following hormones have a stimulatory effect on the intestinal motility but an inhibitory effect on stomach motility?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

CCK is a hormone which is secreted in the duodenum primarily to stimulate the digestion of fat and protein. It has a stimulatory effect on intestinal motility while having an inhibitory effect on stomach motility by delaying gastric emptying. Acetylcholine, gastrin and serotonin both have a stimulatory effect on intestinal and stomach motility. Norepinephrine is primarily a neurotransmitter of the sympathetic system and has an inhibitory effect on intestinal and stomach motility.

The correct answer is B.

Epinephrine reduces contraction in the small and large intestines. One helpful way to remember this is that epinephrine is a neurotransmitter associated with the sympathetic nervous system. When the sympathetic nervous system is activated, the body enters fight-orflight mode and digestion slows down.

stem: Which of the following questions would you ask a patient with dysphagia to best distinguish oropharyngeal dysphagia from esophageal dysphagia?

options.html: Do you have difficulty initiating swallowing or after the action of swallowing?
Do you have difficulty swallowing solid and liquid foods or just solid foods?
Have you encountered any new lumps or bumps in your oral or neck region?
Is the difficulty swallowing progressive or intermittent?

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Esophageal dysphagia is primarily characterized by difficulty swallowing after the initiation of swallowing initiated in the oropharyngeal section. Oropharyngeal dysphagia is characterized by difficulty with the initiation of swallowing. Patients with esophageal dysphagia will thus most likely experience difficulty after the initiation of swallowing, while patients with oropharyngeal dysphagia will experience pain initiating swallowing.

stem: A patient presents to your clinic with dysphagia, odynophagia and acid reflux. A swallow test administered by a speech pathologist reveals the patient has difficulty and pain swallowing both solid and liquid food. Further investigation with high resolution esophageal manometry reveals low to no tonic contractions in the lower esophageal sphincter. Which of the following diagnoses is most likely?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Difficulty swallowing liquids and solids suggest a motility issue over a mechanical issue that might come from a peptic structure or esophageal cancer. The high-resolution esophageal manometry scan measures pressure in the esophagus and acts as a surrogate to measure muscle contraction. The lack of muscle contraction suggests Scleroderma Esophagus where peristalsis does not occur, and the lower esophageal sphincter is perpetually open making the esophagus prone to acid reflux from the stomach. In distal esophageal spasm there is a simultaneous peristaltic contraction throughout the esophagus. Patients with a jackhammer esophagus often experience frequent and repetitive peristalsis movement in their esophagus.

The correct answer is C.

Dysphagia of solids and liquids indicates a motility issue, and the onset of four years indicates a progressive nature. This could be scleroderma or achalasia. stem: Identify the structure of the GI tract that is properly matched with its arterial blood supply.
answer:
The correct answer is D.

The celiac trunk supplies the stomach, and proximal ⅓ of the duodenum (along with the liver, pancreas, and gallbladder). options.html: The proctodeum arises from the endoderm
The liver develops independently from the ventral mesentery and later connects to the midgut
The posterior side of the early embryological foregut eventually becomes the lesser curvature of the stomach
The trachea and the esophagus both develop from the foregut

The correct answer is D.

During week 4 of development, a tracheobronchial diverticulum forms, which eventually leads to the tracheal and esophagus. Option A is false - the proctodeum arises from the ectoderm. stem: A surgeon is performing an appendectomy, which requires him to make an incision through the abdominal wall to remove the inflamed appendix. Which statement below is true?

options.html: The most superficial muscle layer is the external oblique, the middle muscle layer is the transverse abdominis, and the deepest muscle layer is the internal oblique.
An investing fascia surrounds each muscle layer of the abdominal wall.
The deep-most layer of the abdominal wall is the extraperitoneal fat layer.

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Each abdominal wall muscle (external oblique, internal oblique, and transverse abdominis from most superficial to most deep) contains its own investing fascia. The deep-most layer of the anterior abdominal wall is the parietal peritoneum. Camper’s fascia is a superficial fatty layer that does not hold surgical sutures. The stitches were likely placed in the Scarpa’s fascia.

options.html: The left gastroepiploic artery supplies the lesser curvature of the stomach
The splenic artery supplies the spleen and the pancreas
The proper hepatic artery supplies the duodenum
The anterior superior pancreaticoduodenal artery supplies the gallbladder and liver

answer:
The correct answer is B.

The splenic artery branches from the celiac trunk and supplies the pancreas and spleen with oxygenated blood. The lesser curvature of the stomach receives blood from the gastric arteries. The proper hepatic artery supplies the liver, and the pancreaticoduodenal arteries supply the pancreas and the duodenum.

stem: Select the statement that is true:

options.html: CCK is released by the pancreas in response to the presence of proteins and fat in the small intestine
Bile is secreted by gallbladder into the duodenum in order to emulsify fats and promote absorption through the enterocytes.
Histamine stimulates the release of gastrin by G cells and the secretion of acid by parietal cells
Acetylcholine released by the parasympathetic system provides positive stimulation to ECL cells, Gastrin cells, D cells and parietal cells.

answer:
The correct answer is B.

CCK is secreted by duodenal cells in response to the presence of proteins and fats in the small intestine and has the additional functions of delaying gastric emptying and stimulating gall bladder contractions. Gastrin stimulates the release of Histamine by ECL cells and the release of acid by parietal cells. Acetylcholine inhibits D cells and their secretion of somatostatin, which plays a role in reducing stomach acidity.

stem: During a severe H. pylori infection of the antrum of the stomach, many of the D cells die off. Which of the following symptoms may be observed in a patient with a severe H. pylori infection?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

The D cells produce somatostatin, which is primarily released when the stomach contents reach a pH below 3.0, and they have an inhibitory paracrine effect on G cells, ECL cells, and parietal cells to reduce the overall acidity of the stomach. In the absence of somatostatin, the increasing acidity can degrade the epithelial lining of the stomach and lead to ulceration.

stem: A patient presents to your family clinic concerned about their persistent heartburn for the past two months. Which observation allows for a positive diagnosis of GERD?

options.html: A patient’s heartburn is not relieved by antacids or PPIs
An endoscopy does not show signs of erosion in the patient’s esophagus
A 24-hr ambulatory pH monitoring of the patient’s esophagus indicating persistent pH values of 4 or less
A patient points to the center of their chest and claims there’s a burning sensation

answer:
The correct answer is C.

This 24-hour ambulatory pH monitoring showing esophageal pH below 4 indicates gastric acid entering the esophagus (although it would typically be used by patients who have failed a PPI trial). GERD can be erosive; however, 70% of GERD cases are nonerosive. Ordinarily, GERD is confirmed based on symptoms and positive response to a PPI trial.

answer:
The correct answer is D.

In GERD, stomach acid travels superiorly from the stomach to the esophagus, in part because of a dilated lower-esophageal sphincter. Dilatating the esophageal sphincter would exacerbate the patient’s symptoms of GERD.

stem: Which of the following signs and symptoms would be the largest concern for malignancy in a patient with a gastric ulcer?

options.html: A biopsy of the ulcer reveals a round, flat and “punched out” ulcerating region of the stomach
A biopsy reveals the ulcer has raised edges and is an oval appearance
Microscopic analysis of the tissue reveals erosion of the submucosa and the muscularis mucosa as well
The patient experiences symptoms of hemorrhage, regurgitation and radiating back pain

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Some gastric ulcers may be ulcerating cancers. An endoscopy of the ulcer that reveals an oval appearance, with irregular edges, raised edges, and gastric folds that don’t radiate to the edge indicates an ulcerating cancer. An ulcer erodes the submucosa layer as well as the muscularis mucosa layer. The complications of peptic ulcers include hemorrhage, regurgitation, obstruction and radiating back pain.

stem: A 65-year-old patient arrives at your clinic with complaints of heartburn and regurgitation. He states this occurs very intermittently (perhaps once every month), and only after eating a very large meal. The patient currently takes many medications on a daily basis and expresses a strong preference against adding any more regular medications to his routine. The patient has a habit of routinely forgetting to take his medication for sometimes days at a time. Which of the following medications would you likely prescribe this patient for his intermittent GERD?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Antacids are likely the best choice for this patient. Antacids are fast acting and provide symptomatic relief, used in uncomplicated symptoms. Proton pump inhibitors and H2 receptor antagonists would likely need to be included into his regular routine which is not ideal if the patient is only intermittently experiencing symptoms. Furthermore, with H2 receptor antagonists and PPIs patients can experience tachyphylaxis or a rebound effect (from the built-up gastrin) respectively if the patient skips doses.

stem: You are treating a patient with a gastric ulcer. In your investigations to determine the cause of the ulcer you take a brief history which reveals no significant finds other than Warfarin and NSAIDs medication use. A serology test for H. pylori comes back positive, and a C13 Urea Breath Test comes back negative. Based on your investigations, which of the following treatment recommendations do you recommend? Select TWO correct answers.

options.html: Prescribe amoxicillin for H. pylori infection
Prescribe tetracycline for H. pylori infection

answer:
The correct answer is B, C.

Gastric ulcers are commonly caused by NSAID use whereas duodenal ulcers are commonly caused by H. pylori infections. This is further confirmed by the C13 Urea Breath test to determine if there is an active H. pylori infection, the positive serology test indicates that the patient has had H. pylori in the past, but not necessarily currently. A proton pump inhibitor is an appropriate treatment recommendation for both gastric and duodenal ulcers.

For the past two months, he’s had intense upper abdominal pain after eating, and when he was sick with the flu last week, he noticed that his vomit had blood in it. An endoscopy was requisitioned, and the following was observed in his pyloric antrum. What is Regis’s most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

The question stem indicates that the lesion was observed in the pyloric antrum (or in the stomach). Based on the flat, “punched out” appearance, this would likely be a benign gastric ulcer. Note, this is not an erosion as it is clearly a complete breach in the mucosa. Erosions are lesions which are less deep.

stem: There are several classes of drugs that are used to reduce the acidity in the stomach. Which statement below is true?

options.html: Antacids are safe for long-term use with minimal side effects or adverse drug reactions
Prostaglandins reduce the acidity in the stomach by inhibiting proton pumps in the mucosa
H2 receptor antagonists are the most appropriate prescription for the elderly population
PPIs irreversibly inhibit active transport of protons into the lumen of the stomach

answer:
The correct answer is D.

This is the mechanism of action of PPIs. Antacids can have many side effects depending on their composition, from diarrhea to constipation, to drug-drug interactions, etc. Prostaglandins increase the amount of mucus present, protecting the mucosa from stomach acid. H2 receptor antagonists should be prescribed with caution in the elderly population.

options.html: Have more frequent, but smaller meals
Reduce pop and alcohol in the diet
Avoid the use of antiemetic drugs due to the rebound effect

answer:
The correct answer is C.

For patients with gastroparesis, the patient should be educated on having smaller, more frequent meals, reducing pop and alcohol, ceasing smoking, maintaining tight sugar control. To treat the associated symptoms of nausea, antiemetics are prescribed.

stem: Eight weeks ago, Regis was diagnosed with a gastric ulcer. Since then, he has been taking his antibiotic medications to treat the underlying bacterial cause. Today, you are working for a gastroenterologist who has asked you to perform a test to confirm that all of the bacteria has been eradicated. Which test result would indicate an abated infection and would fit with Regis’s history?

options.html: Negative H. pylori IgG serology test

answer:
The correct answer is B.

If Regis had an ulcer caused by H. pylori, even if the bacteria was eradicated, the H. pylori IgG serology test would be positive. Rather, to confirm eradication of the bacterial, a urease breath test should be performed. If negative, it means the infection has subsided.

stem: 54-year-old Taylor arrives at your clinic. She describes how she recently started playing spike ball and has been enjoying it, but this activity is always accompanied by feelings of nausea. Further history leads the physician to suspect motion sickness. Which of the following medications would be most appropriate for Taylor?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Antihistamines (Histamine H1 antagonists) are primarily useful for motion sickness as they act on the vestibular afferents and within the brainstem. 5HT3 receptor antagonists are primarilyused for chemotherapy-induced nausea and post-operative nausea. D2 antagonists are primarily used for nausea induced by toxins and migraine/opioid induced nausea. Cannabinoids are indicated for chemotherapy induced nausea when other agents aren’t working.

stem: A patient arrives at your clinic with concerns of chronic nausea over a period of at least two years. The patient reports this typically occurs after a meal, and often he can’t even finish eating the meal despite what he’s eating. The physician has a strong suspicion for gastroparesis. Which of the following findings would be in line with the physician’s suspected diagnosis?

options.html: An abdominal CT scan showing narrowing at the pyloric sphincter
A gastric emptying study showing delayed gastric emptying at the 4-hour mark

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Gastroparesis is objectively delayed gastric emptying in the absence of a mechanical obstruction. A positive secession splash sign is where the physician listens with their stethoscope to the patient’s belly, and the splashing can indicate signs of obstruction. Cannabis history may be useful in the diagnosis of cannabinoid hyperemesis. An abdominal CT scan showing a mechanical obstruction would point away from the diagnosis of gastroparesis. A gastric emptying study showing severely delayed gastric emptying would be in line with a diagnosis of gastroparesis.

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Brush-border enzymes break down disaccharides into monosaccharides. Salivary amylase is secreted in the mouth and breakdown starch into oligosaccharides. At the level of the small intestine pancreatic amylase breaks down oligosaccharides into disaccharides.

options.html: Increased polysaccharide content in the stool

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Bile salts are reabsorbed in the ileum, along with other fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, and K) and Vitamin B12. With a resected ileum, Gerry will have reduced bile salt reabsorption, and consequently, fatty stool, called steatorrhea.

stem: Several enzymes are responsible for digesting proteins consumed in the diet. Which statement below is true?

options.html: Pepsinogen is secreted by the salivary glands to breakdown oligopeptides
The pancreas secretes trypsin via endocrine mechanisms
Proteins must be broken down into single amino acids to be absorbed
Nine amino acids must be consumed in the diet and cannot be synthesized in the body

answer:
The correct answer is D.

There are nine essential amino acids that the human body cannot synthesize endogenously and must be consumed. Salivary glands secrete salivary amylase to break down oligosaccharides. The pancreas has exocrine and endocrine functions - secretion of trypsinogen occurs via exocrine functions. Lastly, amino acids, dipeptides, and tripeptides are absorbed by the small intestine, where cellular proteases can further digest these into single amino acids.

stem: Which of the following signs/symptoms would you NOT expect to find in a patient with Celiac Disease?

options.html: A duodenal biopsy displaying blunted villi
A duodenal biopsy showing increased inflammation of the bowel
A blood test confirming a deficiency in pancreatic enzymes
HLA typing indicating the patient is positive for HLA-DQ2

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Celiac disease is a malabsorption disease that is due to pathological changes in the mucosal surface of the intestine from an allergic inflammatory reaction to gluten. Thus, a duodenal biopsy may show blunted villi and increased inflammation of the bowels. 95% of patients are positive for HLA DQ2, however this is also fairly prevalent in the general population as well. Patients with Celiac disease may also have a skin rash – dermatitis herpetiformis.

stem: A patient presents to your clinic with a 3-month history of Diarrhea. They describe their stool as large in volume and watery, but not urgent and a normal frequency (2 times per day). The patient does not report any previous infections in the past year and is not taking any medications. The patient however reports feeling of fatigue and weight loss despite his eating habits not changing. Furthermore, a blood test confirms the patient had multiple vitamin deficiencies. Which of the following classifications of the patient’s diarrhea is most accurate?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

The patient’s symptoms have been lasting longer than 4 weeks which suggest a more chronic presentation. Furthermore, the large volume of stool but infrequent and non-urgent presentation signify a small bowel pathology as opposed to a large bowel disorder. The deficiency in vitamins and weight loss suggest a malabsorption/maldigestion issue where the food/vitamins are passed into the bowels and water follows the food content into the bowel creating a watery diarrhea.

stem: At a yearly check-up a patient commented that many of her long-standing dietary issues were resolved after she started avoiding carbohydrates and gluten. For example, bloating and diarrhea stopped after she cut out gluten 4 months ago. For peace of mind, she requests a formal diagnosis of celiac disease – what is the next test that you order?

options.html: Serology testing for tissue transglutaminase (TTG) antibody only
Serology testing for tissue transglutaminase antibody plus IgA levels
Serology testing for IgA levels only
Genetic testing for HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8

answer:
The correct answer is D.

For patients who are currently gluten-free, TTG and IgA levels will not help in elucidating a diagnosis. Gluten-free patients require genetic testing for the human leukocyte antigens HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8. If the patient had recently had gluten in his or her diet, a physician may request serology testing for TTG antibody plus IgA levels. Note that if the TTG antibody levels are low and the IgA levels are low, it’s non-diagnostic.

stem: Which of the following treatment strategies is generally indicated in most cases of infectious diarrhea?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

Aggressive oral hydration is generally indicated in most cases of infectious diarrhea (inflammatory and non-inflammatory) as large volumes of water are lost from the body. Nutrient supplementation may only be appropriate in patients with a malabsorption cause for diarrhea, requiring additional supplements. Antibiotics are not required for most infectious agents causing diarrhea. Antimotility agents are contraindicated in patients with bloody stool or if C. difficile is a consideration, as this can lead to toxic megacolon.

answer:
The correct answer is C.

In this presentation, the clinical suspicion for an E. coli infection is high, particularly due to the risk of eating uncooked beef. In such cases, antibiotics should be avoided, as this can exacerbate hemolytic uremic syndrome.

stem: A patient presents with bloody diarrhea following a 2-week course of clindamycin to treat bacterial pneumonia. A stool culture tests positive for C. difficile. She is 34 years old and is stable. What are the next steps for this patient?

options.html: Prescribe vancomycin for the C. difficile infection
Admit to the hospital, refer to gastroenterologist
Refer to surgery for resection of the offending area

answer:
The correct answer is B.

For C. difficile infections, vancomycin is a good empiric therapy. C. difficile infections are often the result of an antibiotic course of clindamycin. A gastroenterologist may be consulted; however the patient should receive antibiotics for the C. difficile infection immediately.

options.html: A 35-year-old patient with unexplained weight loss

answer:
The correct answer is C.

A colonoscopy for the investigation of constipation should be avoided in patients under the age of 50, unless the patient has red flags such as bloody stool, anemia, weight loss, sudden change in bowel habits or a familiar history of colon cancer.

stem: Which of the following is NOT an appropriate first-line treatment option for a patient with constipation?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

Docusate is stool softener that is generally not recommended due to the lack of evidence for its efficacy. There is low quality evidence for increasing dietary intake and it’s an inexpensive option for many patients. PEG3350 and Lactulose (not PEGLYTE) are both osmotic laxatives used as front-line treatment.

stem: Larry is a 45-year-old who has complaints of constipation. He describes his bowel movements as about once every two days, and nearly all of these require straining. His stool is described as hard and lumpy. He stays hydrated but has a lot of processed foods. His physical exam is relatively unremarkable except reduced bowel sounds. Preliminary blood work is also unremarkable. Based on this presentation, what is the next best recommended treatment for Larry? Choose the best two answers.
answer:
The correct answer is C, E.

Fiber is a good first-line treatment for constipation; patients should be advised to slowly increase fiber in their diet to about 20-30g per day. PEG3350 is an osmotic laxative that retains fluids in the colon and softens stools. Given the lack of any red flags, colonoscopy, defecating proctogram, and anorectal manometry are not indicated.

Archie has a past medical history of narcotic abuse, for which he is currently in recovery. He also takes medications throughout the day to manage his bipolarism. Which medication would you recommend? Select TWO answers.

options.html: None – advise Archie to drink less water

answer:
The correct answer is D, G.

Diarrhea is rarely caused by too much water consumption, so A is not correct. Domperidone and Erythromycin are prokinetics - these would not help the diarrhea but make it worse! Both loperamide and diphenoxylate are opioid antagonists, but diphenoxylate has abuse potential and should be avoided with Archie’s history of narcotic abuse. Cholestyramine is a bile-salt binding resin and would treat the diarrhea; however, this could also cause a negative drug-drug interaction with medication for Archie’s bipolarism. PeptoBismol is generally recognized as safe for most individuals (in rare cases results in neurotoxicity).

stem: You suspect one of your patients has irritable bowel syndrome. Which of the following initial investigations is NOT appropriate for this patient?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

The IgG Food sensitivity test has been widely debunked and should not part of the diagnostic workup for a patient with suspected IBS. IgG production is a normal immune response to food. A fecal Occult Blood stool test can be used to detect the microscopic presence of blood in stool. IBS can have a dramatic impact on the patient’s mental wellness and this should always be a consideration. In patients with red flags (over 50, dysphagia and a history of colon cancer) a colonoscopy can be offered to assess underlying pathologies.

options.html: Pain in the upper part of the abdomen (epigastric pain)

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Functional Dyspepsia is dyspepsia (pain in the upper abdomen) with no evidence of organic disease. Patients can present with postprandial fullness, early satiety, epigastric pain or burning, however all pains must have a negative endoscopy excluding any structural diseases to explain the symptoms.

stem: Which patient below satisfies the Rome IV criteria for irritable bowel syndrome?

options.html: Anthony, who has had two months of abdominal pain associated with defecation with an increase in stool frequency
Bertha, who has had constipation about twice per week, and has 6 months of continuous abdominal pain regardless of her state of constipation
Christopher, who for the past six months has had unbearably painful bowel movements and has noticed streaks of blood upon wiping.

answer:
The correct answer is E.

For IBS according to the Rome IV Criteria, a patient requires having three months of recurrent abdominal pain, and two of: 1) the abdominal pain is related to defecation; 2) a change in stool frequency; and 3) a change in stool appearance. Anthony’s symptoms have not lasted long enough. Bertha’s abdominal pain does not seem to be related to defecation. Christopher’s presentation is more consistent with constipation and hemorrhoids, but not IBS.

Shortly before Eric moved, he was diagnosed with dyspepsia but was unable to discuss treatment options. Which options below would NOT be appropriate for Eric’s management for dyspepsia?

Council the patient on diet modification
Council the patient on exercise reduction to reduce exacerbation of symptoms
Assess Eric’s psychosocial status and consider prescribing antidepressants

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Non-pharmacological treatments of dyspepsia can include lifestyle changes such as improving one’s diet and increasing exercise. Dyspepsia can be caused by an H. pylori infection or by psychosocial factors: antibiotics or antidepressants may be valuable depending on the underlying cause of Eric’s dyspepsia.

stem: A patient arrives at your clinic with concerns of dysphagia, fatigue and weight loss. The patient has previously been diagnosed with GERD. After a thorough history and physical this prompts investigation with endoscopy which reveals an abnormality in the lining of the distal esophagus. Which of the following cancerous tissues is most likely?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Esophageal neoplasms tend to be mostly adenocarcinomas in the west. It’s possible the patient’s GERD may have led to metaplasia of the distal esophageal tissue (Barrett’s esophagus) which may have developed into an adenocarcinoma. Squamous cell carcinoma which is found in the esophagus tends to present in the mid-esophageal region.

stem: A 50-year-old patient presents to your clinic for a colonoscopy after concerns for rectal bleeding and alternating diarrhea and constipation. Lesions were found on the descending colon. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.html: The lesions were likely colorectal polyps and treatment involves surgical removal
The lesions were likely colorectal polyps and treatment involves medical therapy
The lesions were likely serrated adenomas and treatment involves surgical removal
The lesions were likely serrated adenomas and treatment involves medical therapy

answer:
The correct answer is A.

These lesions are likely colorectal polyps as serrated adenomas tend to be more common on the right side (ascending colon). Colorectal cancer is largely preventable through early screening and treatment involves surgical removal of the polyps.

options.html: No, you may have long-term epigastric discomfort but will otherwise be fine.
Chronic GERD could lead to Barrett’s esophagus, which can lead to esophageal cancer.
Chronic GERD could lead to adenocarcinoma, which could lead to Barrett’s esophagus.
Chronic GERD could lead to irritable bowel syndrome if left unchecked.

answer:
The correct answer is B.

GERD can have very severe consequences if untreated, including esophageal cancer (adenocarcinoma). If he cannot afford pantoprazole, perhaps there is a cheaper PPI available that would help with his symptoms, or perhaps the patient qualifies for social supports to help fund this medication.

Colorectal cancers most commonly arise from colitis, although colorectal polyps can also cause colorectal cancers
“Right-sided” colon cancer presents with rectal bleeding and a mass on digital rectal exam
Diagnosis can be made with colonoscopy and biopsy but staging requires X-ray and CT of the chest and abdomen

The correct answer is D.

Stage 4 colorectal cancer indicates that the cancer has spread to the serosa. Almost all colorectal cancers arise from polyps. Lastly, left-sided colorectal cancer presents with rectal bleeding and a mass on DRE, whereas right-sided colorectal cancer presents with anemia and weight loss.

The correct answer is C.

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Endoscopic balloon dilation is the most common treatment for colonic strictures, to dilate the colon. Patient’s may have to do this routinely. Surgical resections are only indicated in the most severe cases due to the risk of contributing to malabsorption.

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Ulcerative Colitis is characterized by lesions that begin at the rectum and extend proximally, thus as an initial investigation only a sigmoidoscopy may be recommended. A colonoscopy is associated with greater risks and is generally done at a later stage to determine the extent of the colon involved. A stool culture and sensitivity test is appropriate in this scenario to rule out any potential infection. A fecal Calprotectin test may also be appropriate to measure the amount of gut inflammation and this can be tracked overtime.

stem: Ulcerative colitis (UC) and Crohn’s disease (DC) are two forms of inflammatory bowel disease. Which statement below is true?

options.html: CD is more likely to be continuous whereas UC is patchy.
UC occurs mainly in the left large bowel; CD occurs mainly in the right large bowel.
Fecal calprotectin will be elevated in patients with UC but not with CD.
None of the above statements are true

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Ulcerative colitis is a continuous inflammation of the large bowel Crohn’s disease is a discontinuous inflammation of the entire GI tract (“gum-to-bum”). Both are inflammatory diseases, and blood tests for both will indicate elevated fecal calprotectin. None of the answers are true statements.

stem: A patient presents to his family doctor with left lower quadrant abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea. Suspecting inflammatory bowel disease, the physician orders a colonoscopy and biopsy of the various locations in the large intestine. Which statement of the pathology report or colonoscopy report is most suggestive of a diagnosis of ulcerative colitis?

options.html: Pathology report: “There is abnormal mucosal physiology of the ascending colon but normal mucosal physiology of the descending colon.”
Pathology report: “Hematoxylin and eosin stain of the tissue sample indicates the presence of granulomas in the mucosa.”
Colonoscopy report: “Shallow ulcers line the descending colon leading to the presence of pseudo-polyps.”
Colonoscopy report: “The inflamed area is patchy and discontinuous.”

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Ulcerative colitis is a continuous inflammation of the large bowel, beginning at the rectum and spreading proximally up the GI tract - if this was UC and there was abnormal physiology in the ascending colon, there would need to be abnormal physiology in the descending colon, so options A and D are false. Granulomas are characteristic of Crohn’s disease, not ulcerative colitis, so option B is false. Ulcerative colitis is associated with shallow ulcers, whereas Crohn’s disease is associated with fissuring ulcers.

stem: A patient presents to your clinic with rectal bleeding that has been ongoing for the past two days. An initial history shows that the patient has been losing a significant amount of blood over the past few days and a CBC shows the patient has become anemic. Which of the following interventional strategies is appropriate?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

During an angiogram a catheter is guided into the mesenteric arteries and contrast is injected to examine the location of bleeding. The angiogram also offers therapeutic potential in circumstances where the patient’s vitals are unstable – the site of the blood site can be determined and therapeutically embolized. An RBC scan or colonoscopy is typically referred for patients who are more stable. An endoscopy is not appropriate for a lower GI bleed.

stem: Which statement below on gastrointestinal bleeding is correct?

options.html: Upper GI bleeds present with melena, whereas lower GI bleeds present with hematochezia
The first step in the management for a patient with GI bleeding is to perform an endoscopy and colonoscopy
Upper GI bleeds occur proximal to the jejunal-ileal junction, whereas lower GI bleeds occur distal to the jejunal-ileal junction
The location of GI bleeding can be deduced at any point in the GI tract via endoscopy or colonoscopy

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Melena (black, tarry stool) is characteristic of an upper GI bleed, occurring proximal to the ligament of Treitz (duodenal-jejunal junction). However, hematochezia (bright red or maroon-colored blood) is characteristic of a lower GI bleed. The first step in any patient with GI bleeding is to assess the patient’s stability and vitals. Note, for the GI bleeding, there are some regions that can’t be reached by endoscopic methods. GI bleeds in these areas are called obscure bleeding.

stem: Which of the following symptoms regarding hemorrhoid are true?

options.html: Patients are likely to notice internal and external hemorrhoid as they’re both painful
Patients are likely to report external hemorrhoid as they can feel it but both internal and external hemorrhoid are painless
Both internal and external hemorrhoid can be associated with blood loss and are both painful
Both internal and external hemorrhoid are associated with blood loss but only external hemorrhoid are painful

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Internal and external hemorrhoids are both characterized by a thrombus of venous circulation that either occur at the anal opening (external hemorrhoids) or occur inside the anus above the pectinate line (internal hemorrhoids). Due to the location of the internal hemorrhoids and their lack of innervation by somatic sensory fibers, they are not painful, while external hemorrhoids are. Both internal and external hemorrhoids are prone to bleeding.

The jejunum and ileum both receive their blood supply from the superior mesenteric artery. The ileum has more mesenteric fat than the jejunum. answer:
The correct answer is C.

stem: Which of the following options regarding colorectal screening is correct?

options.html: Colonoscopy and flexible sigmoidoscopy both require sedation and intensive preparation
Patients who screen positive on a flexible sigmoidoscopy require a follow-up colonoscopy
The feces sample from a FIT test primarily looks for microscopic cancerous tissue
Average risk patients above the age of 50 are offered a colonoscopy every 2 years

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Flexible sigmoidoscopy requires significantly less preparation (an enema the morning of and no sedation) relative to a colonoscopy. Patients who screen positive on a FS must do a colonoscopy to remove all polyps in the distal parts of the colon, which the FS cannot reach. The FIT sample primarily looks for microscopic heme, to detect occult bleeding which can signify the presence of polyps in the colon. Average risk patients above the age of 50 are offered a colonoscopy every 10 years.

His health history is highly suggestive of Crohn’s disease lasting several years, and you are awaiting for some bloodwork to confirm the diagnosis. Given Marc’s family history and positive diagnosis of Crohn’s, what will you recommend for Marc in terms of screening for colorectal cancer?

Marc should undergo a colonoscopy test every five years effective immediately
Marc should undergo a colonoscopy test every two years effective immediately.
Marc should undergo a colonoscopy test every two years that include biopsies effective immediately

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Marc would be considered high risk for colorectal cancer with a first-degree family member having had colorectal cancer. His screening should involve a colonoscopy every two years, with occasional biopsies, beginning ten years earlier than the age of diagnosis of his family member. For low-risk patients, a FIT test every two years is acceptable. For medium-risk patients, the patient should receive a colonoscopy every five years.

stem: In portal hypertension large volumes of venous blood flow through the portal-caval anastomoses in other sites of the body to enter systemic circulation, leading to the development of varicose veins and other site-specific pathologies. Which of the following pathologies are you NOT likely to see in a patient with portal hypertension? Select two options.
answer:
The correct answer is B, E.

External hemorrhoids are not likely because the venous blood supply for this region (below the pectinate line) does not course through the portal system. stem: The gallbladder’s purpose is to both store and concentrate bile. Beginning in the gallbladder, what is the order of structures that bile passes through before entering the duodenum?

options.html: Cystic duct -> common bile duct -> common hepatic duct -> sphincter of Oddi
Common bile duct -> cystic duct -> common hepatic duct -> sphincter of Oddi
Cystic duct -> common bile duct -> pancreatic duct -> sphincter of Oddi
Cystic duct -> common hepatic duct -> pancreatic duct -> ampulla of Vater

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Ascites on percussion has shifting dullness whereas bowel obstruction is tympanic throughout
Ascites present with bowel changes whereas bowel obstructions do not

answer:
The correct answer is C.

You may remember from clinical skills that ascites can be tested by percussion. Laying supine, the side of the patient’s abdomen is percussed medially until tympany is observed. Then, the patient is instructed to shift to a lateral decubitus position and percussion is repeated. If the location at which dullness changes to tympany changes (called shifting percussion), the patient has ascites.

stem: Why is it not recommended to give children plain water to treat dehydration caused by GI pathologies?

options.html: Children enjoy high-sugar fluids more and will likely consume more of those if offered

Dehydration is a necessary physiological process for recovery

answer:
The correct answer is B.

From 05 - Infectious Diarrhea (with 05 - Pediatric Diarrhea). Dehydration is the main complication of diarrhea, and infants are at higher risk. Rehydration should use a balanced electrolyte solution (ORS). Diarrhea loses water and sodium. Replacing that with plain water dilutes the remaining sodium, causing hyponatremia (the same reason tap-water enemas carry a hyponatremia warning in 06 - Constipation). stem: The upper half of the stomach is functionally designed for
answer:
The correct answer is D.

The function of the stomach can be thought of in terms of halves. The lower half of the stomach is primarily responsible for pumping and grinding, metering, peristalsis, and solid emptying. The upper half is primarily responsible for storage of food (acting as a reservoir), stomach contractions, and fluid emptying. Both the upper and lower halves are responsible for acid secretion, as this occurs in the body of the stomach.

stem: Acid secretion in the stomach comes from what cell type?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

Parietal cells are the specialized acid-secreting cells of the stomach. These cells respond to histamine, gastrin, and acetylcholine receptor activation to produce acid. answer:
The correct answer is B.

NSAIDs are the leading cause of gastric ulcers. stem: What of the following is the least common origin of GI bleeds?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Rationally evaluating this list can save you from unnecessary memorization. We can eliminate stomach (A) and the first stage duodenum (D) as these are the common sites of peptic ulcers, which are a common problem (not to mention gastric varices and many other causes). Likewise, we can eliminate the colon (B) because it is the most common site of lower GI bleeds. We must now decide between the cecum and the jejunum. Small bowel bleeds outside of the first stage duodenum and the terminal ileum rare. stem: What is a possible complication of a choledochal cyst?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

A choledochal cyst is a congenital dilation of the common bile duct. The dilation predisposes the duct to bile stasis allowing for infection to occur. stem: What is the pathogenesis of the development of carcinoma from a choledochal cyst?

options.html: Bile stasis → deconjugated bile acids → bacteria overgrowth → metaplasia → dysplasia →cancer

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Dilation of the bile duct predisposes to the duct to bile stasis. Bile stasis permits bacteria growth within the duct and as the bacteria proliferate they deconjugate the bile acids. Deconjugated bile within the duct system, along with infection and inflammation, lead to metaplastic changes within the cells forming the duct. Metaplastic changes lead to dysplastic changes, and finally full blown carcinoma (cholangiocarcinoma) can occur.

stem: Which structure would bleed if cut in surgery?
answer: C) Lateral umbilical fold. The median umbilical fold is the obliterated urachus (the urachus is a remnant of the allantois which sends waste to the placenta during the first 7 weeks gestation. Once the cloaca ruptures and starts dumping waste into the amniotic fluid, there is no need for the allantois for waste removal and it obliterates into the urachus). The medial umbilical fold is the obliterated umbilical artery (during development the umbilical artery carries deoxygenated blood from the fetus to the placenta, after birth once the neonate is breathing on its own the vasculature connection to mom is obliterated). The lateral umbilical fold contains the inferior epigastric vessels (which would bleed if cut). The superior umbilical fold does not exist.

stem: Which of the following is FALSE about slow wave electrical activity in the GI tract?

options.html: It is dependent on innervation from the enteric nervous system
Slow wave refers to the spontaneous variation at rest of the muscle fibre

answer:
The correct answer is A.

Slow waves are not dependent on innervation by the enteric nervous system, so A is false. This is because the slow waves are spontaneous variations in the membrane potential of the smooth muscle fibres at rest (D). These spontaneous variations of muscle are therefore independent of nervous system activity. Answers B and C are also correct. The ICC coordinate their pacing of slow waves to ensure GI tract contents are propagated away from the mouth (B). Although the ICC cannot generate a contraction, they coordinate contractions by determining the frequency and timing of slow waves, which are in turn required for an action potential or a contraction to occur (C).

stem: A 5-year-old child presents to the emergency department with a 2-day history of abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea. On examination, the child appears pale and dehydrated. Laboratory tests reveal hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury, consistent with a diagnosis of hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS). What is the appropriate management for this patient? Select all that apply.
answer: The correct options are A), C), and D). Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) is a potentially life-threatening condition characterized by hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury. It is most commonly caused by Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC) infection, which is often associated with diarrhea. A) Fluid resuscitation is a critical initial management step for HUS to maintain adequate organ perfusion and prevent further renal injury. B) Antibiotics are not routinely recommended for HUS caused by STEC infection. In fact, some studies suggest that antibiotics may actually increase the risk of HUS development by increasing the release of Shiga toxin. C) Blood transfusion may be necessary to correct severe anemia and maintain adequate oxygen delivery to the tissues. D) Dialysis may be necessary in patients with severe acute kidney injury and fluid overload. E) Antidiarrheals are not recommended in HUS because they may prolong the duration of bacterial shedding and increase the risk of complications. F) Platelet transfusion is not typically necessary in HUS because thrombocytopenia is usually mild and self-limited. In fact, platelet transfusion may increase the risk of thrombotic complications.

answer:

stem: You are in the Emergency Room when a 45 year old man arrives presenting with vague RUQ pain. You notice he is slightly jaundiced during inspection and upon physical exam he demonstrates tenderness in the right upper quadrant. In your investigation, you order Hepatitis B serology. The results come back as: -ve HBsAg, +ve anti-HBs, +ve anti-HBe, +ve anti-HBc, -ve HBeAg. What does this say about his condition.

options.html: He has been vaccinated and immunized against HepB previously but never got it
He has had an acute flare of HepB.
He has not been immunized against HepB nor has gotten the disease in the past
He is a chronic carrier of HBV

answer:
The correct answer is A.

HbsAg is a marker of acute or chronic infection; since this is negative, this individual does not currently have a Hepatitis B infection. anti-HBc is the antibody against the core protein, which indicates that this individual had a previous exposure (because we know he/she is not infected now). From these two findings alone, we can answer the question (A - previously infected). anti-HBs is positive, but could be positive if someone had recovered from an infection or had been vaccinated. anti-HBe is positive, which means this person has clinically recovered from a Hep B infection and is immune (since we know she/he is not currently infected). HBeAg is negative, which means this person is not infective at present, consistent with our previous findings.

Her blood work showed normal bilirubin and mildly elevated ALT, AST, ALP. What is the appropriate first line imaging modality?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

An abdominal U/S is the best imaging modality in this case due to several reasons. An abdominal U/S will give you a general idea of how this patient’s abdomen will look, including all the organs in the area. It is cheap, fast, and removes the need for the patient to be exposed unnecessarily to radiation. You are also able to look at the soft tissue structures of the region, including details of the biliary tree, check for signs of inflammation, obstruction, or stones. You are not able to do this in such detail with abdominal X-ray, HIDA, or ERCP. Without further indications, abdominal CT would also be inappropriate.

answer:
The correct answer is E.

The key features to this patient’s presentation are: she is female, mildly jaundiced, elevated AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin, and a positive ANA. Given these features, this patient is most likely suffering from autoimmune hepatitis. Several of the other options can be ruled out, such as primary sclerosing cholangitis (D) (mostly young men, not women). Hemochromatosis (B) is more likely to present with bronzing of the skin, and older than 16 in women because of menstruation (natural phlebotomy, if you will). In Wilson’s disease (A), you would not expect autoimmune markers to be positive, and there would be a salient family history of psychiatric illness.

The correct answer is A.

stem: A 54-year-old man comes in presenting with jaundice and dark urine. He has a 12 pack of beer per day alcohol drinking history. Lab results come in with AST 400, ALT 250, alkaline phosphatase 120, total bilirubin of 31 µg/L, and direct bilirubin of 12 µg/L. What is his most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

Alcoholic hepatitis is most likely given the heavy drinking history presented. Additionally, his AST is greater than his ALT and both are under 500, which is a common set of lab results for alcoholic hepatitis. Gilbert’s syndrome (B) would be characterized by stress-induced jaundice, normal liver enzymes, and a high total but low direct bilirubin, probably 20% or less of the total. While hemolysis (C) may present with elevated bilirubin, it’s less likely given the elevated liver enzymes and history. Viral hepatitis (E) would present with an ALT>AST, and generally both would be elevated past 1000.

options.html: Delirium secondary to hepatocellular carcinoma brain metastasis

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Of the options presented, hepatic encephalopathy secondary to alcohol intoxication is the most likely cause of his symptoms. The decreased LOC and asterixis are caused by the accumulation of ammonia and other toxins in the blood after liver failure. The history of hepatitis C would have predisposed him to both encephalopathy and hepatocellular carcinoma (B) but HCC doesn’t commonly spread to the brain. stem: Which of the following is the most common cause of chronic pancreatitis in North American adults?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

Alcoholism is the most common cause of chronic pancreatitis in North American adults, causing >90% of cases. This is due to the changes in the pancreas caused by alcohol, including the increased viscosity of the pancreatic juices, decreased pancreatic secretion of pancreatic stone protein, and acinar and duct cell toxicity. Unusual causes include CF, severe protein-calorie malnutrition, hereditary and idiopathic reasons. Gallstones only cause acute pancreatitis, not chronic cases.

stem: What is not a possible complication of choledocholithiasis?
answer:
The correct answer is E.

Complications of choledocholithiasis include bile duct stricture, cholangitis, pancreatitis, and biliary cirrhosis. However, it does not cause acute cholecystitis because by definition, cholecystitis is an inflammation of the gallbladder resulting from sustained gallstone impaction in the cystic duct or Hartmann’s pouch, whereas choledocholithiasis involves stones in the common bile duct, further down the tract.

stem: A 35-year-old female patients presents in the emergency with a 3 day history of severe epigastric pain that radiates to her back along with nausea, vomiting, and fever. You immediately suspect acute pancreatitis and order lab-work to confirm your diagnosis. The results come back as (normal ranges in brackets): Hb 133 (120-160), WBC 18 (4-11), lipase 16000 (<150), ALT 19 (<20), AST 37 (<35), ALP 116 (50-160), random glucose 12 (4.0-7.8), LDH 203 (50-150). Which of the above values is the LEAST predictive of you patient’s mortality with acute pancreatitis?
answer:
The correct answer is E.

Based on Ranson’s Criteria for acute pancreatitis, it is useful to look at the following five factors at time of admission to predict the course of the disease. They are a) Age >55yrs, b) WBC >16, c) Glucose >11, d)LDH >350, and e) AST >250. Thus, while lipase is a useful investigative tool, it is not necessarily helpful as a predictive value.

stem: Which of the following does not have the potential to cause conjugated hyperbilirubinemia?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Gilbert’s disease is a problem of unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, not conjugated. This is because the enzyme responsible for conjugation is sluggish or deficient. Pregnancy (A) can lead to conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, usually early in pregnancy as a benign recurrence of cholestasis, or late in pregnancy as acute fatty liver of pregnancy or preeclampsia. Miliary TB (C) can cause obstruction of bile outflow (among other multi-organ problems) that would present with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Pancreatic cancer (D) can lead to conjugated hyperbilirubinemia if, for instance, the tumour compresses the bile duct. Biliary atresia (E) is a common cause of conjugated hyperbilirubinemia in infancy.

stem: Which of the following is not a risk factor for cholelithiasis?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Females are more prone to cholelithiasis than males as estrogen is an important risk factor. In addition, obesity and being <50y/o (Age) also are risk factors. Being on TPN causes impaired gallbladder emptying, thus facilitating stone formation, and rapid weight loss cause rapid cholesterol mobilization and biliary stasis which can also increase the chances of gallstone development. A common way to think about the risk factors for gallstones is the 4F’s: Fat, Female, Fertile, Forties.

stem: A 47-year-old Caucasian woman comes to your clinic with a complaint of weight loss, epigastric pain, and diarrhea with foul smelling stool that started “a little while ago”. She also notes that she’s concerned about the weight loss but just seems to be turned off food as eating seems to make the pain worse. Bloodwork reveal hyperglycemia and elevated INR. She denies smoking but admits to regular alcohol consumption. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

The most likely cause of this patient’s presentation is chronic pancreatitis. Clues to this diagnosis include: chronic alcohol use; persistent epigastric pain; diarrhea, foul-smelling stools, and weight loss, all of which can be attributed to poor fat digestion due to insufficient pancreatic enzyme secretion or production; and apparent diabetes, which can result from severe cases of chronic pancreatitis in which the beta cells are destroyed or cannot produce enough insulin. T2DM (A) or Celiac disease (B) on their own are not enough to explain the constellation of symptoms, although malabsorption and hyperglycemia are features of this patient’s presentation. Peptic ulcer disease (D) would explain her epigastric pain relating to meals, but would present with anemia and black stools, rather than diabetes and foul-smelling stools. A bowel obstruction (E) is also inconsistent with the symptoms, and would likely feature bilious vomiting.

stem: Match each of the following to either ALT > AST or AST > ALT.
answer:
The pairings:

ConditionEnzyme pattern
NAFLDALT > AST
Acute Budd-Chiari syndromeAST > ALT
Alcoholic liver diseaseAST > ALT
Viral hepatitisALT > AST
Celiac diseaseALT > AST
Ischemic hepatitisAST > ALT

From 03 - Approach to Abnormal Liver Enzymes. AST is found outside the liver (muscle, red cells, brain) and falls in mitochondria-heavy, alcoholic, ischemic or vascular injury; ALT is the more liver-specific enzyme and dominates in most inflammatory or metabolic hepatocellular injury. The lecture's lists sort each item:

  • NAFLD = ALT > AST: steatosis and NASH are ALT-predominant.
  • Acute Budd-Chiari = AST > ALT: hepatic venous outflow obstruction behaves like ischemic or congestive injury.
  • Alcoholic liver disease = AST > ALT: classically at 2:1 or more.
  • Viral hepatitis = ALT > AST: acute or chronic.
  • Celiac disease = ALT > AST: a systemic cause of mild ALT elevation.
  • Ischemic hepatitis = AST > ALT, grouped with congestive hepatopathy.

stem: Which of the following statements accurately describes the anatomical relationship between the portal vein and the hepatic artery?

options.html: The portal vein is located anterior to the hepatic artery.
The portal vein and the hepatic artery run parallel to each other throughout their course.
The portal vein and the hepatic artery run adjacent to each other in a common sheath.
The portal vein and the hepatic artery have no anatomical relationship and do not share a common pathway.

answer: C) The portal vein and the hepatic artery run adjacent to each other in a common sheath. Explanation: The portal vein and the hepatic artery are the two main vessels that supply blood to the liver. While they do not directly communicate with each other, they are intimately related in their course to the liver. The portal vein is formed by the union of the splenic and superior mesenteric veins and runs adjacent to the hepatic artery in a common sheath as they enter the liver. This close anatomical relationship is important in the regulation of blood flow to the liver and helps to ensure that the liver receives adequate oxygenated blood from the hepatic artery and nutrient-rich blood from the portal vein.

stem: Which of the following laboratory findings is most commonly associated with cirrhosis
answer: D) Elevated levels of bilirubin Explanation: Cirrhosis is a chronic liver disease characterized by progressive scarring and fibrosis of the liver tissue. As liver function declines in cirrhosis, there is impaired processing and excretion of bilirubin, leading to elevated levels of this pigment in the blood. Bilirubin is a waste product produced by the breakdown of red blood cells, and high levels can cause yellowing of the skin and eyes (jaundice). While elevated levels of AST and ALT can also be seen in liver disease, they are not specific to cirrhosis and can be elevated in many types of liver injury. Elevated levels of ALP can be seen in liver disease as well as bone disease and other conditions, and are not specific to cirrhosis.

stem: In hepatitis B infection, which of the following hepatitis B virus (HBV) serological markers indicates a chronic infection?

options.html: HBsAg positive, anti-HBc positive, anti-HBs negative
HBsAg negative, anti-HBc positive, anti-HBs positive
HBsAg positive, anti-HBc positive, anti-HBs positive
HBsAg negative, anti-HBc negative, anti-HBs negative

answer: A) HBsAg positive, anti-HBc positive, anti-HBs negative Explanation: In hepatitis B infection, the presence of HBV serological markers can indicate the different stages of infection. HBsAg (hepatitis B surface antigen) is the first serological marker to appear and indicates acute infection. If HBsAg persists for more than 6 months, it indicates chronic infection. Anti-HBc (hepatitis B core antibody) is a marker of previous or ongoing infection with HBV, and can be positive in both acute and chronic infection. Anti-HBs (hepatitis B surface antibody) is a marker of immunity to HBV and is produced in response to vaccination or past infection. In chronic hepatitis B infection, the patient is HBsAg positive for more than 6 months, anti-HBc positive, and anti-HBs negative. In the other options, the patient is either not infected (D), has recovered from past infection or been vaccinated (B), or has an unclear stage of infection (C).

stem: A 45-year-old male presents with fatigue, joint pain, and abnormal liver function tests. Further evaluation reveals elevated serum ferritin levels and genetic testing confirms a diagnosis of hemochromatosis. What is the recommended treatment for this patient?
answer: B) Phlebotomy Explanation: Hemochromatosis is a hereditary disorder characterized by excessive accumulation of iron in the body, leading to tissue damage and organ dysfunction. The primary treatment for hemochromatosis is phlebotomy (bloodletting), which aims to remove excess iron from the body. In the initial phase of treatment, weekly or biweekly phlebotomy is recommended until iron levels are reduced to normal levels. Once normal iron levels are achieved, the frequency of phlebotomy can be decreased to every few months to maintain normal iron levels. Iron supplementation (A) is contraindicated in hemochromatosis as it can exacerbate iron overload. Corticosteroids (C) may be used in certain cases of hemochromatosis-related liver disease, but they are not the primary treatment. Chelation therapy (D), which is commonly used to treat iron overload in thalassemia, is not effective in hemochromatosis as it does not remove iron from the liver.

stem: Which of the following are contraindications to transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS)? There may be more than one correct answer.
answer: A) Hepatic encephalopathy and D) Severe coagulopathy Explanation: TIPS is a procedure that involves creating a shunt between the portal vein and hepatic vein to reduce portal hypertension in patients with cirrhosis and related complications. However, TIPS is not suitable for all patients, and there are several contraindications to the procedure. Hepatic encephalopathy is a common complication of cirrhosis and is a contraindication to TIPS as it can worsen after the procedure. Severe coagulopathy, such as an INR greater than 2.5, is also a contraindication to TIPS as the procedure can lead to bleeding complications. Severe pulmonary hypertension (B) is not a direct contraindication to TIPS, but it can increase the risk of complications during the procedure. Advanced liver cirrhosis (C) is also not a direct contraindication, but it can decrease the efficacy of the procedure and increase the risk of complications.

stem: A 55-year-old male presents to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain that radiates to his back, vomiting, and fever. Laboratory testing reveals elevated serum lipase and amylase levels. CT scan demonstrates pancreatic inflammation and fluid collections. What is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
answer: B) Pancreatitis Explanation: The patient's symptoms and laboratory findings are highly suggestive of acute pancreatitis, which is a sudden inflammation of the pancreas that can be caused by various factors, including alcohol consumption, gallstones, high triglyceride levels, infections, and certain medications. Abdominal pain is the hallmark symptom of pancreatitis and is often severe and persistent, radiating to the back. Nausea, vomiting, fever, and elevated serum lipase and amylase levels are common features of pancreatitis. CT scan is a valuable imaging modality to confirm the diagnosis and assess the severity of the disease. Pancreatic cancer (A) typically presents with more subtle symptoms and is often detected at a later stage when the disease has already spread. Pancreatic pseudocyst (C) is a complication of chronic pancreatitis and presents with a palpable abdominal mass and obstructive symptoms. Pancreatic duct obstruction (D) can cause chronic pancreatitis, but it is not the primary cause of acute pancreatitis.

From 10 - Upper and Lower GI Bleeding. Active bleeding is a main indication for endoscopy, not a contraindication. After resuscitation, urgent EGD is "both diagnostic and therapeutic" (epinephrine injection, cautery, hemoclips, variceal banding). In lower GI bleeding, stable patients go on to colonoscopy.

  • Suspected perforation (A): insufflating air through a perforated viscus worsens the leak. Free air is a surgical emergency (04 - Abdominal Pain).
  • Obstruction (B): bowel prep cannot pass, and a distended bowel risks perforation.
  • Fixed or redundant colon (C): the scope cannot be advanced safely, which raises the perforation risk.
  • Recent MI (E): sedation and the procedure put stress on an unstable heart.

stem: Which of the following is not a symptom of functional dyspepsia?

stem: A 65-year-old female presents to the emergency department with abdominal pain, distention, and vomiting. On examination, she has hyperactive bowel sounds in the upper abdomen and hypoactive bowel sounds in the lower abdomen. What type of bowel obstruction is more likely in this patient?
answer: A) Small bowel obstruction Explanation: The clinical presentation of small bowel obstruction and large bowel obstruction can overlap, but there are certain features that can help distinguish between the two. Small bowel obstruction typically presents with more severe abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and rapid onset of symptoms, while large bowel obstruction may present with more chronic or intermittent symptoms such as constipation, bloating, and lower abdominal pain. On examination, hyperactive bowel sounds in the upper abdomen and hypoactive bowel sounds in the lower abdomen are more suggestive of a small bowel obstruction as the obstruction typically occurs proximal to the ileocecal valve. In contrast, a large bowel obstruction usually presents with high-pitched bowel sounds in the lower abdomen due to distension and accumulation of gas and stool. Gastric outlet obstruction (C) can cause similar symptoms to small bowel obstruction but typically presents with more prominent vomiting and epigastric pain. Colonic volvulus (D) is a type of large bowel obstruction that presents with colicky abdominal pain, obstipation, and distension, and may be associated with a palpable mass on examination.

stem: A 50-year-old male presents to the emergency department with left lower quadrant abdominal pain, fever, and nausea. On examination, there is tenderness and guarding in the left lower quadrant with no rebound tenderness. CT scan of the abdomen shows sigmoid colon diverticulitis without evidence of perforation or abscess. What is the most appropriate management for this patient?
answer: B) Antibiotics alone Explanation: The clinical presentation of diverticulitis includes left lower quadrant abdominal pain, fever, nausea, vomiting, and change in bowel habits. CT scan is the imaging modality of choice for the diagnosis of diverticulitis and to assess for complications such as perforation or abscess. In cases of uncomplicated diverticulitis without evidence of perforation or abscess, the mainstay of treatment is antibiotics alone. Patients with mild to moderate symptoms can be treated on an outpatient basis, while those with severe symptoms or comorbidities may require hospitalization. Observation and supportive care (A) alone are not sufficient for the treatment of diverticulitis. Surgical consultation (C) may be needed in cases of complicated diverticulitis, but it is not indicated in uncomplicated cases. Percutaneous drainage of abscess (D) is indicated in cases of complicated diverticulitis with abscess formation. Colonoscopy (E) is contraindicated during an acute episode of diverticulitis, as it may increase the risk of perforation.

stem:
A 24-year-old presents with 2 weeks of diarrhea with blood and mucus. They report frequent, small-volume stools and abdominal cramping.

What is the most likely mechanism?
answer: The correct answer is C. Deck: bloody diarrhea = inflammatory → large intestine involvement → cytotoxin-mediated damage (e.g., Shigella, EHEC). The Infectious Diarrhea lecture agrees: inflammatory diarrhea is cytotoxin-mediated invasion of the colonic mucosa (blood or mucus, frequent small stools); enterotoxin-mediated diarrhea is small-bowel, watery and high-volume.

stem:
A 30-year-old with intermittent bloating and diarrhea is suspected of having celiac disease, but symptoms are atypical and serology is equivocal. You want to rule out the diagnosis.

What is the best next test?
answer: The correct answer is D. Deck: HLA testing is most sensitive and used to rule out celiac if negative. Essentially every celiac patient carries HLA-DQ2 or DQ8, so their absence excludes it; a positive result proves little (DQ2 is common in the general population). Duodenal biopsy remains the definitive diagnosis when you are trying to rule it in. Checked against the course GI QBank celiac items and the GI review session.

stem:
A 28-year-old with mild Crohn’s disease presents with RLQ pain and diarrhea. No systemic complications.

What is first-line treatment?
answer: The correct answer is D. Deck: mild Crohn’s → budesonide (local steroid) is first-line (5-ASA is for mild UC). The IBD lecture: mild ileitis and right-sided colitis → budesonide, a glucocorticoid with a large hepatic first-pass effect, almost as effective as prednisone with far fewer side effects; oral 5-ASA helps only a small percentage of Crohn patients. Prednisone, azathioprine and methotrexate are for moderate–severe disease.

A patient has been prescribed an opioid for their severe pain and asks for treatment for chronic constipation

Which of the following should be avoided?
answer: The correct answer is D. Deck: stool softeners (docusate) are not recommended and ineffective. The Constipation lecture’s Choosing Wisely slide: don’t use stool softeners alone to prevent opioid-induced constipation – docusate was no better than placebo for stool frequency or consistency. PEG and magnesium (osmotic) and senna (stimulant) are the effective choices.

stem: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of milk of magnesia?

options.html: Draws water into the bowel via osmosis

answer: The correct answer is C. Deck: magnesium-based laxatives = osmotic → pull water into gut. The Constipation lecture lists magnesium-based agents with PEG 3350 and lactulose as osmotic laxatives (watch magnesium in kidney disease). Stimulants (senna, bisacodyl) act on enteric nerves; secretagogues (linaclotide) increase secretion; docusate/mineral oil soften/lubricate; fibre adds bulk.

A 35-year-old patient with a 10-year history of ulcerative colitis presents for routine follow-up. They are currently asymptomatic.

What is the most appropriate colorectal cancer screening strategy?

options.html: Colonoscopy now and repeat every 1–3 years
No screening required unless symptoms develop

answer: The correct answer is C. Deck: IBD → start screening 8 years after diagnosis, then colonoscopy every 1–3 years (much higher risk from chronic inflammation). The IBD lecture: regular colonoscopic biopsy surveillance beginning at 8 years, every 1–3 years, end-point = dysplasia. FIT and age-50 colonoscopy are average-risk strategies.

A 68-year-old patient is admitted after a large stroke. They have severe dysphagia and are unable to safely swallow. They are expected to require nutritional support for the next 2 weeks.

What is the most appropriate nutritional support?
answer: The correct answer is B. Deck: short-term (< 3 weeks) → enteral feeding; high aspiration risk → avoid NG (stomach); use post-pyloric feeding (NJ) to reduce aspiration risk; TPN only if the gut is not usable. The Nutrition lecture lists strokes as an indication for both NG and NJ tubes, with NJ specifically for risk of aspiration with oral and NG feeding; gastrostomy is for long-term (> 6 weeks) feeding.

Elevated direct (conjugated) bilirubin
Markedly elevated ALP and GGT

answer: The correct answer is B. Deck: ↑ ALP + GGT → cholestatic pattern; conjugated bilirubin supports obstruction or a bile-flow problem. Abnormal Liver Enzymes lecture: ALT/AST = hepatocellular injury; ALP (confirmed hepatic by GGT) = cholestasis. Hemolysis would raise unconjugated bilirubin.

answer: The correct answer is B. Deck: first-line = lactulose (traps ammonia in the gut, increases excretion); rifaximin = add-on if recurrent or refractory; don’t jump to transplant unless King’s criteria are met; measuring ammonia or urea is unreliable. A 72-year-old with atrial fibrillation presents with sudden severe abdominal pain. On exam, the abdomen is soft with minimal tenderness despite severe pain.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is B. Deck: pain out of proportion to exam = acute mesenteric (arterial) ischemia; classic in AF → embolic. The appendix is a true diverticulum

answer: The correct answer is C. Eosinophilic esophagitis: young males, atopy, food bolus impaction, furrows and rings. Dx = > 15 eosinophils/HPF in the mid esophagus; treat with PPI, swallowed topical steroids, dilation and food elimination. Goblet-cell metaplasia = Barrett esophagus.

A 3-week-old breastfed infant is still jaundiced. He is feeding and growing well.

What is the most appropriate next step?
answer: The correct answer is D. Physiologic jaundice (low UGT1A1 at birth) peaks days 2–5. Jaundice persisting beyond 2 weeks needs total and conjugated bilirubin without delay: conjugated hyperbilirubinemia → prompt referral for biliary atresia, where timely Kasai surgery matters. Phototherapy/exchange is for a rapidly rising unconjugated bilirubin (> 340 μmol/L).

A 70-year-old with a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass has cholangitis from an obstructing hilar stricture; endoscopic access to the papilla failed.

What is the best procedure to image and drain the bile ducts?
answer: The correct answer is A. PTC = percutaneous transhepatic cholangiogram. MRCP is diagnostic only – it cannot offer therapy. ERCP is diagnostic and therapeutic but needs endoscopic access (Roux-en-Y anatomy is a limitation). PTC is indicated when ERCP is contraindicated or failed, gives the best view of the proximal tree and allows percutaneous drainage.

stem:
A 50-year-old heavy drinker has 2 years of recurrent epigastric pain after meals and greasy stools. CT is equivocal.

Which test is the most sensitive for chronic pancreatitis?
answer: The correct answer is E. Chronic pancreatitis is diagnosed by imaging – there are no good blood tests (lipase/amylase are often normal). CT/MRI is most commonly used; endoscopic ultrasound is the most sensitive. Calcification on x-ray/CT is specific but late; HbA1c screens for the diabetes that follows > 90% loss of function.

answer: The correct answer is E. Primary prophylaxis by screening EGD: no varices → repeat in 2–3 years; small varices → repeat in 1–2 years (NSBB if high risk); large varices → NSBB or endoscopic variceal ligation. Octreotide, tamponade and TIPS are for acute bleeding.
